documents.title: FINRA Adopts Amendments to Rule 3220 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others)
documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA, as part of its FINRA Forward modernization initiative, has amended Rule 3220 (the Gifts Rule) effective March 30, 2026. The amendments raise the annual gift limit from $100 to $300 per recipient, codify and clarify prior interpretive guidance, and authorize exemptive relief. New supplementary material defines valuation and aggregation standards, clarifies supervision and recordkeeping obligations, and delineates categories of gifts that are excluded from the $300 cap and recordkeeping requirements: personal gifts for infrequent life events, bereavement gifts, de minimis and logo promotional items, commemorative items commemorating a business transaction (even if over $300), and certain disaster-relief donations. The rule is confirmed not to apply to gifts to a member‚??s own associated persons or to individual retail customers. FINRA also adopts conforming $300 gift limits in Rules 2310, 2320, 2341, and 5110, aiming to modernize the regulatory framework while maintaining investor protection and providing flexible, risk-based supervisory expectations.

documents.enrichment_summary: GD Culture Group (GDC) has received board approval to sell part of its 7,500-bitcoin reserve, currently valued at about $497 million, in order to help fund a previously announced $100 million stock repurchase program. The authorization gives management full discretion over the timing and amount of any bitcoin sales and can be altered or halted at any time. GDC is sitting on an unrealized loss of $344 million on its bitcoin holdings, which were accumulated via the acquisition of Pallas Capital Holding, financed through issuance of 39.18 million shares. The company‚??s share price is up about 7% on the day amid a modest rebound in bitcoin to above $67,000, but remains nearly 70% below its September 2025 peak. Other crypto-related firms, such as Bitdeer and Riot Platforms, have also been reducing or liquidating bitcoin holdings. Separately, MetaMask is rolling out its blockchain-based, non-custodial debit card across the U.S. after a year-long pilot, enabling users to spend digital assets directly from self-custodial wallets anywhere Mastercard is accepted, including via Apple Pay and Google Pay, in a competitive market that already includes Visa-linked products.

documents.title: Normally staid bond investors have a new biggest worry: An AI bubble
documents.speaker: CNBC
documents.enrichment_summary: The article reports that concerns about a potential artificial intelligence (AI) bubble have become the top perceived risk among bond investors, according to Bank of America Global Research's February credit investor survey. For the first time, an AI bubble ranks above other risks, with 23% of respondents naming it their biggest worry, up from 9% in December. Investors expect a sharp increase in bond issuance from large technology "hyperscalers" such as Amazon and Google parent Alphabet, projecting about $285 billion in high-grade credit issuance this year versus $210 billion previously. Despite these fears, only 10% of surveyed investors cite AI-driven corporate obsolescence as their main concern, indicating more anxiety around market froth and financing needs than long-term disruption. The piece contrasts bond investors' relatively muted worries about geopolitics and central bank policy errors, even amid U.S.-Iran tensions and an upcoming change in Federal Reserve leadership, and notes that AI disruption has already weighed heavily on certain software stocks and sector ETFs, which remain significantly down year-to-date.

documents.enrichment_summary: The article reports that Bitcoin Standard Treasury Company (BSTR), led by early Bitcoin pioneer Adam Back, is moving ahead with plans to go public via a SPAC merger with Cantor Equity Partners I (CEPO), targeting shareholder approval as soon as April 2026 despite sharp declines in bitcoin and bitcoin treasury stocks. BSTR plans to list with 30,000 BTC on its balance sheet, 25,000 BTC from Back and founding shareholders and 5,000 BTC contributed in-kind by early investors. Back argues that bitcoin‚??s recent price drop is driven by macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty rather than regulatory pressure and could actually benefit BSTR by allowing it to accumulate more bitcoin at lower prices ahead of listing. He maintains that bitcoin treasury companies, whose core strategy is to buy and hold BTC, ultimately remove supply from the market and thus act as a long‚??term bullish catalyst, even though their accumulation tends to slow in bear markets.

documents.title: SEC approves WisdomTree plan for 24/7 trading of tokenized money market fund
documents.speaker: CoinDesk
documents.enrichment_summary: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) granted WisdomTree exemptive relief to allow its Treasury Money Market Digital Fund (WTGXX) to trade at a fixed $1 intraday price with a broker-dealer, instead of only at end-of-day NAV. Under the new model, a broker-dealer trades from its own inventory on a 24/7 basis with instant blockchain settlement, while the mutual fund structure and regulatory framework remain unchanged. WisdomTree also introduced continuous, on-chain dividend accrual that allocates yield based on wallet holding time, initially targeting institutional users via its Connect platform and potentially retail users via its Prime app. This development is framed as part of a broader, now $10 billion, tokenized U.S. Treasury market led by firms such as BlackRock, Circle, and Ondo Finance, where tokenization is used to speed settlement and reduce operational friction while keeping traditional regulatory oversight.

documents.title: Ethereum Foundation starts 70,000 ETH staking process to fund operations, bolster network
documents.speaker: CoinDesk
documents.enrichment_summary: The Ethereum Foundation has begun staking 70,000 ETH from its treasury to generate rewards that will fund protocol research, ecosystem development, and community grants. The process started with a 2,016 ETH deposit and uses Dirk and Vouch, open-source validator tools from Attestant, to distribute signing and validator duties across multiple jurisdictions and reduce single points of failure. This move follows the public release of the Foundation's treasury policy, which aims to balance long-term financial sustainability with Ethereum-aligned values such as decentralization, open-source access, and user privacy. The staking setup combines hosted infrastructure and self-managed hardware, including minority clients, deployed in several countries. With an estimated staking yield of around 2.808% according to the CoinDesk Composite Ether Staking Rate (CESR), the Foundation is putting a portion of its roughly 172,650 ETH (plus 10,000 WETH) holdings to productive use rather than leaving them idle.

documents.speaker: CoinDesk
documents.enrichment_summary: Austria's Financial Market Authority (FMA) has ordered KuCoin EU to immediately stop conducting new business and onboarding customers across the EU after the exchange lost key compliance staff just months after receiving a Markets in Crypto Assets (MiCA) license. The regulator said KuCoin EU no longer has suitable key function holders for anti-money laundering (AML), terrorist financing prevention, and financial sanctions compliance, roles that were a prerequisite for its November authorization. KuCoin says it is expanding its compliance team in Austria, emphasizing a "compliance-first" model and hiring experienced local professionals. Austria continues to attract crypto exchanges using MiCA passporting, with firms like Bitpanda, Bybit, and Bitget also basing operations in Vienna, while KuCoin, a Seychelles-based exchange founded in China in 2017, remains among the top global centralized platforms by trading volume.

documents.title: Pacificorp Agrees to Pay $575 Million to Settle Claims for Damage Caused by Six Wildfires in Oregon and California
documents.speaker: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Oregon
documents.enrichment_summary: The U.S. Department of Justice announced that PacifiCorp agreed to pay $575 million to settle federal claims that its electrical lines negligently started six major wildfires in Oregon and California in 2020 and 2022. The settlement reimburses substantial federal wildfire suppression costs and funds restoration of approximately 290,000 acres of burned public lands managed by the U.S. Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management. Officials emphasize that the agreement provides fair compensation to taxpayers while preserving PacifiCorp's ability to provide affordable electricity and aligns with DOJ policy to hold entities responsible for wildfire damages. The settlement resolves civil claims without any determination of liability, and PacifiCorp continues to deny responsibility for the fires.

documents.title: Frederick Man Charged With Violating National Defense Airspace
documents.speaker: U.S. Attorney's Office, District of Maryland
documents.enrichment_summary: The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Maryland announced that 66-year-old Stuart Bennett of Frederick, Maryland, has been charged with violating national defense airspace by allegedly flying a drone (Unmanned Aircraft System) over sensitive U.S. national defense facilities and posting the footage on a YouTube channel titled "Area 82 Surveillance911." A joint FBI and NCIS investigation linked the channel and videos, which included purported imagery of Department of Defense facilities, critical national security infrastructure, and locations labeled as "classified" or "Top Secret," to Bennett through IP address data, recovery phone numbers, and USPS-registered email addresses. A subsequent search of Bennett's residence resulted in the seizure of a Potensic Atom drone, micro-SD cards, and a computer system, including a monitor displaying the YouTube channel logged in; at least one SD card allegedly contained video of a drone flight over the Raven Rock Mountain Complex. The case highlights federal enforcement of airspace restrictions around national defense installations and collaboration between the FBI, NCIS, and Pentagon Force Protection Agency.

Officials from the Department of Justice, Department of Labor OIG, HHS-OIG, and the Tennessee Department of Human Services emphasized their commitment to protecting pandemic relief programs and pursuing fraudsters.

documents.enrichment_summary: The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Texas announced that Carol Talamantes, a 61-year-old certified public accountant in El Paso, was sentenced to 33 months in federal prison for wire fraud. Between October 20, 2020, and October 31, 2024, she stole approximately $603,738.96 from multiple real estate businesses in Texas and New Mexico by issuing fraudulent company checks to herself, making unauthorized electronic transfers and ACH transactions to her own accounts, and using the funds for personal expenses such as her home mortgage and credit card bills. Talamantes pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud on September 26, 2025, agreed to a money judgment for the full loss amount, and had previously been released on a $20,000 bond. The FBI investigated, and Assistant U.S. Attorney Phillip Countryman prosecuted the case.

documents.title: BELL MAN PLEADS GUILTY TO MAKING NUMEROUS THREATS TO KILL NEWSPAPER REPORTER, MUSLIMS, AND POLITICIANS
documents.speaker: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida
documents.enrichment_summary: The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Florida announced that Peter Daniel Ring, 31, of Bell, Florida, pleaded guilty in federal court to sending multiple interstate threats to kill or cause physical injury against at least fourteen victims, including a Washington Post reporter, Muslims, media members, and prominent politicians. After initially being warned by the FBI in June 2025 following a death threat to a reporter, Ring continued to post religiously and politically motivated threats between May and September 2025. He faces up to 10 years in prison, with sentencing set for April 28, 2026, before Chief U.S. District Judge Allen C. Winsor in Gainesville. The case, investigated by the FBI and prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Christie S. Utt, is part of Operation Take Back America, a Department of Justice initiative targeting illegal immigration, cartels, transnational criminal organizations, and violent crime.

documents.title: PENSACOLA MAN PLEADS GUILTY TO DRUG DISTRIBUTION AND ILLEGAL WEAPONS CHARGES
documents.speaker: U.S. Attorney's Office, Northern District of Florida
keywords: felon in possession of a firearm
Assistant U.S. Attorney Jessica S. Etherton
documents.enrichment_summary: The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Florida announced that Damian Elliott Pressley, 38, of Pensacola, pleaded guilty in federal court to three counts of distributing more than 50 grams of methamphetamine, possession with intent to distribute cocaine and marijuana, and possession of a firearm and ammunition as a convicted felon. The charges stem from multiple methamphetamine distributions in October and November 2024 and a December 2024 search of his Pensacola residence that yielded a loaded firearm, significant quantities of marijuana and cocaine, and cash. Due to prior convictions, Pressley faces a mandatory minimum of 15 years and up to life in prison, with sentencing set for May 7, 2026, before U.S. District Judge T. Kent Wetherell II. The case was investigated by the DEA and prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Jessica S. Etherton and is part of Operation Take Back America, a Department of Justice initiative aimed at combating illegal immigration, cartels, TCOs, and violent and drug-related crime.

documents.title: Sen. Warren tells Fed and Treasury: No bailout for crypto billionaires
documents.speaker: CNBC
documents.enrichment_summary: The article reports that Sen. Elizabeth Warren sent a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell urging them to commit that no taxpayer funds will be used to bail out "cryptocurrency billionaires and other highly leveraged cryptocurrency investors" amid a sharp bitcoin selloff of about 50% since its October high. Warren argues that any intervention to stabilize Bitcoin would be unpopular, would effectively transfer wealth from taxpayers to wealthy crypto holders, and could personally benefit President Donald Trump and his family through their crypto firm, World Liberty Financial, which has been active in managing leveraged positions during the downturn. She highlights that Treasury and the Fed possess crisis-support authorities that could, in theory, be deployed to support crypto-related entities, and criticizes Bessent for not clearly ruling out such use when questioned in Congress. Warren further calls on federal financial agencies to strengthen protections for retail crypto investors, citing a record $17 billion in crypto fraud losses in 2025, and lists major losses by prominent crypto investors as evidence of the current market distress.

documents.title: Treasury yields rise as Fed minutes show disagreement on next rate cut
documents.speaker: CNBC
documents.enrichment_summary: The article reports that U.S. Treasury yields rose after Federal Reserve meeting minutes revealed internal divisions over the timing and necessity of the next interest rate cut. The 10-year yield climbed to about 4.087%, the 30-year to 4.711%, and the 2-year to 3.468%, with all moving a few basis points higher. While policymakers broadly agreed to keep rates unchanged in January at 3.5%‚??3.75%, they were split on future policy, debating whether to prioritize labor-market conditions or inflation. Some officials favored holding rates steady for an extended period and questioned whether further policy easing was warranted without clearer evidence that disinflation progress was securely back on track. Fed Chair Jerome Powell emphasized a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach, and investors were awaiting the upcoming PCE price index release, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, for additional insight on the economic outlook.

documents.title: What Will Artificial Intelligence Mean for the Labor Market and the Economy?
documents.speaker: Governor Michael S. Barr
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Michael S. Barr argues that artificial intelligence, particularly generative AI, is likely to be a general-purpose technology with substantial long-run benefits for productivity, innovation, and living standards, but with potentially painful short-run disruptions for specific worker groups and sectors. He outlines three scenarios for AI's evolution: (1) gradual diffusion with strong but manageable productivity gains and limited, temporary joblessness; (2) a rapid "jobless boom" with widespread displacement, rising unemployment, and major distributional and social challenges; and (3) stalled progress and overinvestment, where AI's productivity impact is modest and risks shift toward financial stress. Current evidence and early research are most consistent with the first, gradual-adoption scenario: aggregate employment and wages have not yet moved significantly, but early-career workers in AI-exposed occupations appear to be adversely affected, AI is driving task-level productivity gains and internal job reallocation rather than mass layoffs, and inequality impacts remain uncertain. documents.speaker: CNBC
documents.enrichment_summary: The article reports that the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield was largely unchanged at around 4.058% on Tuesday in a holiday-shortened week, as investors awaited delayed economic data releases. The 30-year Treasury yield slipped to about 4.689%, while the 2-year yield rose to roughly 3.439%. Trading is described as quiet following the Presidents' Day market closure. Investors are focused on upcoming Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) minutes for clues on the prior interest rate decision and future monetary policy, alongside delayed housing data for November and December and the December personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge. Futures markets, via the CME FedWatch Tool, indicate a 92% probability that the Federal Reserve will leave the federal funds rate unchanged in the 3.5%‚??3.75% target range.

documents.title: Nicholas Bowerman
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained a default final judgment against Nicholas Bowerman, former finance director at CIRCOR International's U.K. unit Pipeline Engineering, for alleged accounting fraud that caused CIRCOR to overstate its financial performance by millions of dollars between 2019 and 2021. The SEC's complaint alleges Bowerman falsified internal records, account reconciliations, certifications, and bank confirmations, and misled management and auditors, resulting in inflated consolidated financial statements. The judgment permanently enjoins him from violating multiple antifraud, books-and-records, and internal controls provisions of the federal securities laws, bars him from accounting, financial reporting, and audit roles for public companies, and orders disgorgement of $17,823.80 plus $4,148.51 in prejudgment interest and a $75,000 civil penalty. The matter was investigated and litigated by staff in the SEC‚??s Philadelphia Regional Office.

documents.title: John David Gessin et al.
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained default final judgments in the Central District of California against John David Gessin, Equifunds, Inc., and Ice Fleet LLC for a multi‚??year fraudulent scheme that raised over $1.6 million from five retail investors. The complaint alleged that Gessin misrepresented that investor funds would be used solely for business purposes but instead diverted funds for personal expenses such as a home mortgage, cars, hotels, and gifts. The court permanently enjoined all defendants from violating antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws and imposed joint and several liability for $1,230,807 in disgorgement plus $410,116 in prejudgment interest. Gessin was additionally barred from participating in most securities activities, prohibited from serving as an officer or director of a public company, and ordered to pay a $945,804 civil penalty. The matter was investigated and litigated by staff from the SEC Division of Enforcement.

documents.title: U.S. DOJ hits Paxful for $4 million in case tied to illegal sex work, money laundering
documents.speaker: CoinDesk
documents.enrichment_summary: The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) secured a $4 million criminal penalty against former peer-to-peer bitcoin marketplace Paxful Holdings after the company pleaded guilty to facilitating illegal prostitution, violating anti-money-laundering (AML) laws, and knowingly handling criminal proceeds. Prosecutors had initially contemplated a $112 million penalty, but the amount was reduced based on Paxful's inability to pay. Paxful, which shut down in 2023, had processed up to $3 billion in crypto trades between 2017 and 2019, including transactions for Backpage, an online advertising platform associated with illicit sex work. U.S. Attorney Eric Grant emphasized that platforms ignoring criminal activity will face serious legal consequences. Separately, prediction market firm Kalshi sanctioned two users, including a MrBeast employee, for alleged insider trading based on nonpublic information about MrBeast's content, suspending and fining them. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) highlighted Kalshi's actions in an advisory as potential law violations and described exchanges like Kalshi as a first line of defense against insider trading.

documents.title: Treasury yields fall after retail sales miss expectations
documents.speaker: CNBC
documents.enrichment_summary: The article reports that U.S. Treasury yields declined after December retail sales came in flat, missing expectations for a 0.4% month-on-month increase. The 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields each fell by more than 5 basis points to 4.141% and 4.781%, respectively, while the 2-year yield dropped more than 3 basis points to 3.452%. Commentator Todd Schoenberger interprets the weak holiday sales as a sign of low consumer confidence and stretched credit, warning that the economic margin for error is thin. Markets are now focused on a backlog of U.S. economic data delayed by the partial government shutdown, including the January nonfarm payrolls report, consumer price index data expected to show slightly cooler 2.5% annual inflation, and weekly jobless claims. The piece also notes that investors are watching China after reports that Chinese authorities have encouraged banks to reduce exposure to U.S. Treasurys due to concentration risk and volatility.

documents.title: 10-year Treasury yield is little changed as investors await busy week of economic data
documents.speaker: CNBC
documents.enrichment_summary: The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield started the week essentially unchanged at 4.20%, alongside minimal moves in the 30-year (4.854%) and 2-year (3.487%) yields, as investors awaited a backlog of key U.S. economic data delayed by a partial government shutdown. The January nonfarm payrolls report, now due Wednesday, is expected to show a 55,000 job gain with unemployment steady at 4.4%, while Friday's delayed January CPI release is forecast to show annual inflation easing to 2.5%. Additional data on December retail sales (Tuesday) and weekly initial jobless claims (Thursday) are also in focus. Markets are further monitoring reports that Chinese authorities have urged domestic banks to scale back U.S. Treasury purchases over concentration and volatility concerns, with mainland China‚??s Treasury holdings reportedly down 11% over the past year to $682.6 billion.

documents.title: CBA Pharma, Inc., Wayne Michael Putnam, Louis A. Carmichael
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed a civil enforcement action in the Eastern District of Kentucky against CBA Pharma, Inc., its president Wayne Michael Putnam, and vice president of capital markets Louis "Buzz" Carmichael, alleging they conducted a fraudulent securities offering that raised about $4.1 million from roughly 160 investors. From April 2023 to February 2024, the defendants allegedly misrepresented that CBA Pharma's only drug, CBT-1, was effective against cancer by preventing multidrug resistance and was in the final stages of FDA approval, despite the FDA having found insufficient evidence of efficacy and having withdrawn the drug application by April 2023. The complaint charges violations of Securities Act Section 17(a) and Exchange Act Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5, and seeks permanent injunctions, disgorgement with interest, civil penalties, and participation bars for the individual executives. The investigation and litigation are being handled by staff in the SEC's Chicago Regional Office, with assistance from the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Kentucky, the FBI's Louisville Field Office, and the FDA.

documents.title: Economic Outlook and Supply-Side (Dis)Inflation Dynamics
documents.speaker: Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson
documents.enrichment_summary: Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson offers a cautiously optimistic outlook for the U.S. economy, highlighting a stabilizing labor market, resilient growth around 2.2 percent, and stalled but expected-to-resume disinflation toward the Federal Reserve's 2 percent inflation target. He explains that inflation progress in 2025 was held back largely by higher tariffs boosting core goods prices even as services inflation, especially housing, eased. Jefferson supports the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC) recent decision to hold the federal funds rate after a cumulative 175 basis-point reduction since mid-2024, arguing policy is now broadly around a neutral stance and appropriately balanced between maximum employment and price stability. The core of the speech analyzes supply-side (dis)inflation dynamics, drawing lessons from pandemic-era disruptions, global shocks, and the limitations of traditional Phillips-curve models in explaining the inflation surge. He underscores that structural productivity growth has recently strengthened, potentially enabling robust output and real wage gains without added inflation, driven by new business formation, high-tech activity, and emerging AI adoption.

documents.title: Ryan Squillante
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained a final consent judgment against Connecticut resident Ryan Squillante in a civil enforcement action for insider trading. Squillante allegedly used confidential information from his employment at an investment firm to trade in securities of at least ten publicly traded companies, earning approximately $216,965 in illegal profits. The final judgment permanently enjoins him from violating Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Rule 10b-5, and orders disgorgement of $216,965 plus $33,800 in prejudgment interest, which are deemed satisfied by the criminal fine imposed in a parallel criminal case, United States v. Squillante. The investigation was conducted by staff in the SEC's Boston Regional Office and the Market Abuse Unit, with assistance from FINRA.

documents.title: Gerald Shvartsman; Michael Shvartsman; Rocket One Capital LLC
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained final consent judgments against brothers Gerald and Michael Shvartsman in a civil insider trading case involving securities of Digital World Acquisition Corporation (DWAC). The SEC had alleged that they traded DWAC securities based on material nonpublic information about DWAC's merger negotiations with Trump Media & Technology Group, realizing net profits of approximately $4.64 million and $18.27 million, respectively. The final judgments permanently enjoin both defendants from violating antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws. Gerald Shvartsman must disgorge $4.64 million and Michael Shvartsman $18.27 million, with both disgorgement obligations deemed satisfied by forfeiture orders in parallel criminal cases. The judgment against Michael also imposes an officer and director bar. The SEC voluntarily dismissed its action against Rocket One Capital LLC. The litigation was handled by staff of the Division of Enforcement's Market Abuse Unit and the New York Regional Office.

documents.title: Marat Likhtenstein
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed and settled civil charges against investment adviser Marat Likhtenstein for operating a self-issued promissory note scheme that raised over $4.1 million from at least 15 advisory clients, many elderly and primarily from the Russian-American Jewish community. The complaint alleges that from 2017 to 2024 he falsely promised extraordinary returns from lucrative business opportunities but did not invest client funds, instead misappropriating them, including $940,000 in Ponzi-like payments and nearly $3.2 million for personal expenses. The SEC charged violations of antifraud provisions of the Securities Act, Exchange Act, and Investment Advisers Act, seeking disgorgement, prejudgment interest, civil penalties, and conduct-based and anti-fraud injunctions. Likhtenstein consented, without admitting or denying the allegations, to a bifurcated settlement providing for injunctive relief, with monetary remedies to be decided later; the court entered the consent judgment on February 4, 2026. A parallel criminal case was brought by the Kings County District Attorney‚??s Office, and the SEC acknowledges that office‚??s assistance.

Bowman explains why she supported the FOMC‚??s January 2026 decision to hold the federal funds rate at 3.5‚??3.75 percent, emphasizing a cautious, data-dependent approach as policy moves toward a neutral stance. She judges current policy as moderately restrictive and projects three rate cuts in 2026 but prefers to implement them at a measured pace to preserve flexibility and "keep policy powder dry" while assessing how last year‚??s easing is affecting broader financial conditions and the labor market.

Bowman describes an economy that continues to expand at a solid pace with improving inflation dynamics but a labor market she characterizes as increasingly fragile. She notes that GDP growth was strong in Q3 2025 but likely slowed in Q4 due to the government shutdown and softer consumer spending, with residential investment still weak. documents.title: Statement by Governor Christopher J. Waller
documents.speaker: Governor Christopher J. Waller
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Christopher J. Waller explains his dissent at the most recent FOMC meeting, arguing that a 25 basis point cut to the policy rate was warranted. He contends that, despite solid overall economic growth, the labor market is weak, with near-zero payroll growth in 2025 compared to an average of 1.9 million jobs per year over the prior decade, rising unemployment, and reports of planned layoffs. He views this as evidence of subdued labor demand and a significant risk of labor market deterioration. Waller also notes that while headline inflation is elevated due to tariff effects, underlying inflation excluding those effects is close to the FOMC's 2 percent target and expectations remain anchored. Given weak labor conditions and inflation near target, he argues policy should move closer to the estimated neutral rate of 3 percent, rather than remaining 50‚??75 basis points above it, to support the labor market and preempt further deterioration.

documents.title: Vikram Luthar
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC has filed a civil enforcement action against former Archer-Daniels-Midland Company (ADM) executive Vikram Luthar, alleging that he orchestrated accounting and disclosure fraud while serving as CFO of ADM's Nutrition segment and later as ADM's overall CFO. According to the complaint, when the Nutrition segment failed to meet publicly touted operating profit growth targets for fiscal years 2021 and 2022, Luthar allegedly directed improper, retroactive intersegment pricing adjustments‚??such as rebates and price changes not typically available to third-party customers‚??to shift operating profit from other ADM business segments to Nutrition. These actions allegedly made ADM's disclosures about intersegment pricing false and misleading and caused material overstatements of Nutrition's operating profit and growth in ADM's 2021 and 2022 periodic reports. The SEC charges Luthar with violations of antifraud, reporting, books and records, internal controls, and Sarbanes-Oxley clawback provisions, and seeks permanent injunctions, an officer and director bar, disgorgement with interest, civil penalties, and reimbursement of certain executive compensation to ADM.

documents.title: Anil Mathews; Rahul Agarwal; Kenneth M. Harlan; and MobileFuse, LLC

documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed a civil enforcement action in the Southern District of New York against former Near Intelligence, Inc. CEO Anil Mathews and former CFO Rahul Agarwal for allegedly orchestrating a round‚??trip accounting and disclosure fraud scheme that overstated Near's revenue by an average of 27% between May 2021 and September 2023, including at least $37.3 million in improperly reported revenue tied to its largest customer, MobileFuse, LLC. The complaint alleges Near and MobileFuse exchanged grossly inflated invoices so Near could recognize fictitious revenue, concealed the scheme from auditors through fabricated documents and misstatements, and that Mathews misappropriated over $300,000 to rent a luxury residence. MobileFuse and its former CEO, Kenneth M. Harlan, are charged with aiding and abetting the alleged fraud. The SEC seeks permanent injunctions, officer and director bars, civil penalties, and disgorgement (with prejudgment interest) from Mathews, and acknowledges assistance from multiple U.S. and foreign authorities.

documents.title: Regulations, the Supply Side, and Monetary Policy
documents.speaker: Governor Stephen I. Miran
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Stephen I. Miran argues that recent and prospective deregulation‚??especially in the United States and exemplified earlier by Greek structural reforms‚??has substantial supply-side effects that monetary policymakers must explicitly incorporate. He maintains that regulations can severely constrain productive capacity, distort investment, impede firm entry, and raise prices through both lower total factor productivity and higher markups. Advances in measuring regulation using NLP and AI show a sharp reduction in U.S. regulatory restrictions in 2025, and Miran projects that roughly 30 percent of federal regulatory restrictions will be removed by 2030, partly due to a "one-in-ten-out" executive order. Citing empirical work, he estimates that the resulting deregulation could reduce the U.S. consumer price level by about 3 percent by 2030 relative to baseline, implying material downward pressure on inflation. Because he views deregulation as primarily expanding potential output faster than actual output, he concludes that it widens the output gap and warrants a more accommodative monetary stance, including lower policy rates, even as it may raise the neutral real interest rate. documents.title: Statement from Federal Reserve Chair Jerome H. Powell
documents.speaker: Chair Jerome H. Powell
documents.enrichment_summary: In this statement, Federal Reserve Chair Jerome H. Powell announces that the Department of Justice has served the Federal Reserve with grand jury subpoenas threatening a criminal indictment related to his June Senate testimony on a multi-year renovation of historic Fed office buildings. Powell asserts respect for the rule of law and accountability, but characterizes the subpoenas as an unprecedented action that must be viewed in the broader context of administration threats and pressure. He argues that the stated focus on his testimony and building renovations is a pretext, and that the real issue is retaliation for the Fed setting interest rates according to evidence and economic conditions rather than the President's preferences. Powell frames the situation as a test of whether monetary policy will remain independent or be directed by political pressure or intimidation. He notes his service under four administrations of both parties and reaffirms his intention to continue performing his duties, emphasizing integrity, independence, and the Fed's mandate of price stability and maximum employment.

documents.title: Caroline Ellison, Gary Wang, and Nishad Singh

documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC announced that it has filed proposed final consent judgments in the Southern District of New York against Caroline Ellison (former CEO of Alameda Research Ltd.), Zixiao "Gary" Wang (former CTO of FTX), and Nishad Singh (former Co-Lead Engineer of FTX). The underlying complaints alleged that, between May 2019 and November 2022, Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX raised over $1.8 billion from investors through false claims that FTX was a safe trading platform with robust automated risk controls and that Alameda Research had no special privileges. In reality, Alameda was allegedly exempted from risk mitigation measures, given a virtually unlimited line of credit funded by FTX customer assets, and enabled‚??through software code created by Wang and Singh‚??to access and divert customer funds. Ellison allegedly used misappropriated customer funds for Alameda trading, while hundreds of millions more in customer assets were allegedly funneled to Alameda for venture investments and loans to Bankman-Fried and other executives, including Wang and Singh. Without admitting or denying the allegations, Ellison, Wang, and Singh agreed to permanent injunctions against violating key antifraud provisions

documents.title: George John Drazenovic
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed a settled civil enforcement action in the Southern District of New York against George John Drazenovic, a Canadian and British Columbia-licensed chartered professional accountant, alleging that he recklessly furthered two penny stock rings' multimillion-dollar pump-and-dump schemes from at least April 2010 to October 2019. The complaint asserts that Drazenovic located mineral extraction or exploration rights that were used as marquee assets for at least ten penny stock issuers, while allegedly disregarding that the controlling rings had no genuine intention to develop the mineral projects and instead used promotional campaigns to inflate stock prices before dumping their shares and using some proceeds to pay him. Drazenovic, without admitting or denying the allegations, consented to a proposed final judgment, subject to court approval, that would enjoin him from violating antifraud provisions of the Securities Act and Exchange Act, impose a conduct-based injunction limiting his ability to induce securities transactions to larger-cap, publicly traded securities, permanently bar him from penny stock offerings, bar him from serving as an officer or director of a public c

documents.title: Danh C. Vo
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed a civil enforcement action in the District of Delaware against Danh C. Vo, founder and CEO of VBit Technologies Corp., alleging that he fraudulently raised over $95.6 million from about 6,400 investors through bitcoin mining "Hosting Agreements" and misappropriated $48.5 million for personal use, including gambling and gifts to family members, before fleeing the U.S. The SEC alleges Vo lied about VBit's business, assets, and use of investor funds, and that VBit sold hosting capacity for more mining rigs than it actually operated. The complaint charges Vo with registration and antifraud violations under the Securities Act and Exchange Act, and seeks permanent injunctions, disgorgement with prejudgment interest, a civil penalty, and an officer and director bar. Vo's family members are named as relief defendants and have consented to final judgments, subject to court approval, requiring disgorgement of ill-gotten gains. The matter was investigated and will be litigated by staff in the SEC's Division of Enforcement, including the Market Abuse Unit and Cyber and Emerging Technologies Unit.

documents.title: Mina Tadrus
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained a final consent judgment against Florida resident Mina Tadrus in a civil enforcement action involving a fraudulent investment scheme that targeted members of the Egyptian Coptic Christian community. From at least September 2020, Tadrus and his controlled entity, Tadrus Capital LLC, raised over $5 million from at least 31 investors for Tadrus Capital Fund LP by falsely claiming investor funds would be pooled and invested using algorithmic trading to guarantee steady monthly returns. The SEC alleged that most investor funds were not invested, about $1.4 million was used to make Ponzi-like payments of the promised returns, and over $380,000 was misappropriated for Tadrus‚??s personal benefit. The court had previously issued a preliminary injunction and asset freeze in August 2023, and in August 2025 entered a bifurcated consent judgment permanently enjoining Tadrus from violating multiple antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws, imposing a conduct-based injunction restricting his securities activities, and imposing an officer-and-director bar. The final consent judgment orders disgorgement of $4,070,350 plus $72,100 in prejudgment interest, deemed satisfied

documents.title: Fred W. Wagenhals, Robert D. Wiley, and Christopher D. Larson
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed a civil enforcement action in the District of Arizona against former Ammo, Inc. (now Outdoor Holding Co.) executives Fred W. Wagenhals, Robert D. Wiley, and Christopher D. Larson for alleged accounting and disclosure fraud. The complaint alleges Wagenhals (former CEO) and Wiley (former CFO) repeatedly made materially false and misleading statements in Ammo‚??s SEC filings and financial statements to conceal unfavorable information about the company‚??s management and operations, including the undisclosed executive role of co-founder Larson. Despite a 2020 federal court order barring Larson from serving as an executive at a public company, the SEC alleges he secretly played a critical senior management role, led a major acquisition, and arranged transactions that financially benefited himself or family members. The SEC charges all defendants with violations of antifraud provisions under the Securities Act and Exchange Act, and additionally charges Wagenhals and Wiley with falsifying books and records, lying to auditors, providing false certifications, and failing to reimburse compensation under Sarbanes-Oxley Section 304(a). documents.title: Artur Khachatryan
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed and simultaneously settled an enforcement action against Artur Khachatryan of Tujunga, California, alleging a two‚??year manipulative spoofing scheme in thinly traded stocks that generated approximately $373,885 in illicit profits. According to the complaint, Khachatryan placed large spoof orders outside regular market hours to move stock prices, then executed genuine trades on the opposite side of the market to profit from the artificial price movement before canceling the spoof orders, repeating the process in both directions. After several broker‚??dealers restricted or closed his accounts, he allegedly opened brokerage accounts in the names of other individuals to continue trading. The SEC charged violations of Securities Act Section 17(a), Exchange Act Sections 10(b) and 9(a)(2), and Rule 10b‚??5. Without admitting or denying the allegations, Khachatryan consented to a final judgment (subject to court approval) imposing permanent injunctions, disgorgement of $373,885 plus $22,629.34 in prejudgment interest, a $112,165 civil penalty, and a four‚??year restriction on opening or using brokerage accounts without providing broker‚??dealers a copy of the judgment. documents.title: James O Ward, Jr.
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained a final judgment against Alabama private fund manager James O. Ward, Jr. in a civil enforcement action alleging an offering fraud tied to Apex Financial Institute Pvt. Ltd. Ward was accused of making multiple material misrepresentations to approximately 70 investors, raising at least $852,000, including false claims about SEC regulation, assets under management, prior beta testing, risk-free substantial gains, and international offices. Without admitting or denying the allegations, Ward had earlier consented to a court order permanently enjoining him from violating key antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws, limiting his securities trading to listed securities in his personal accounts, and barring him from serving as an officer or director of a public company. The court has now imposed an $85,000 civil penalty, as requested by the SEC, with the matter handled by SEC Enforcement staff in the Atlanta Regional Office.

documents.title: Irfan Mohammed
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed and simultaneously settled a civil enforcement action against Peoria, Illinois resident Irfan Mohammed for allegedly conducting an offering fraud targeting members of the Islamic community in Central Illinois. From January 2021 through March 2023, Mohammed allegedly raised about $585,000 by falsely claiming his company, Dgtal World LLC, operated a successful overseas payment processing business expanding into the U.S., when in fact the company had no operations. The complaint alleges he misappropriated investor funds for an unrelated business and personal expenses and made sham and Ponzi-like payments to investors to create the illusion of returns. Mohammed, without admitting or denying the allegations, consented to a judgment charging violations of Securities Act Section 17(a), Exchange Act Section 10(b), and Rule 10b-5. The proposed settlement, subject to court approval, includes a permanent injunction against future violations, a conduct-based injunction barring him from most securities activities outside his personal account, disgorgement of $385,220 plus $70,640 in prejudgment interest, and a $70,000 civil penalty. The investigation was conducted by SEC staff Liz

documents.title: Charles D. Oliver; David P. Ortiz; DaveGlo Investment Group, Inc.; Kevin N. Richards
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed three related civil enforcement actions on September 11, 2025, against Florida-based investment adviser and insurance agent Charles D. Oliver, California-based adviser David P. Ortiz and his entity DaveGlo Investment Group, Inc., and former California insurance agent and adviser Kevin N. Richards. The complaints allege that, from at least 2020 through 2021, the defendants marketed and sold approximately $82 million in risky, unregistered oil and gas securities to around 95 retail investors, acted as unregistered brokers, and failed to disclose financial conflicts of interest. Oliver allegedly used his "Hidden Wealth Radio" show to solicit about $52 million in investments and received over $4.3 million in transaction-based compensation. Ortiz and DaveGlo allegedly raised about $18 million through mass marketing, including radio commercials, earning Ortiz more than $800,000 in transaction-based compensation. Richards allegedly raised about $12 million using mass marketing and his own radio show and received over $600,000 in transaction-based compensation. The offerings were sponsored by companies and principals previously charged in the SEC's Resolute Capital Partners m

documents.title: Tiffany Kelly and Curastory Inc.
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed and simultaneously settled an enforcement action against Curastory Inc. and its founder/CEO Tiffany Kelly, alleging an offering fraud in which they raised about $2.8 million from over 1,000 investors by repeatedly misrepresenting the company‚??s revenues, projected financial performance, and purported million‚??dollar investments, and by forging a prospective investor‚??s signature. The complaint charges violations of the antifraud provisions of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b‚??5 under the Exchange Act. Without admitting or denying the allegations, Curastory and Kelly consented to permanent injunctive relief; Kelly also agreed to a $125,000 civil penalty, a ten‚??year conduct‚??based injunction restricting her participation in securities transactions (other than for her personal accounts), and a ten‚??year bar from serving as an officer or director of a public company, subject to court approval.

documents.title: The Inflation Outlook
documents.speaker: Governor Stephen I. Miran
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Stephen I. Miran argues that underlying U.S. inflation is now close to the Federal Reserve's 2 percent target once measurement distortions in shelter and imputed service prices are removed, and that monetary policy is therefore too tight and should be eased more quickly. He expects PCE shelter inflation to fall faster because market rents have been flat for two years, PCE shelter has overshot new-tenant rents, population growth has weakened, and shelter‚??s share of nominal consumption is historically elevated and mean-reverting. For core nonhousing services, he downplays concern, emphasizing that labor markets have loosened and wage growth has slowed, while a large part of recent measured services inflation comes from nonmarket, imputed items such as portfolio management fees. He argues these fees are mismeasured: industry data show fee deflation while PCE imputations show sharp increases, which he calls "phantom" inflation that should not drive policy. Turning to core goods, Miran is skeptical that recent increases are primarily tariff-driven. documents.title: Kevin L. Jefferson and Demetrius L. Early
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained final consent judgments against Texas residents Kevin L. Jefferson and Demetrius L. Early for their roles in a fraudulent, unregistered securities offering that raised over $1 million from more than 65 investors, primarily targeting members of the African American community in Shreveport, Dallas, Houston, and elsewhere. From January to December 2023, Jefferson, through his Cashflow Creation Club and with Early as a primary sales agent, allegedly promised investors expert Forex trading and monthly returns of 3‚??5% that could grow to about $83,000 per month, but instead misappropriated nearly 85% of investor funds for undisclosed commissions and personal expenses. Without admitting or denying the allegations, both defendants consented to final judgments that permanently enjoin them from violating securities registration and, for Jefferson, antifraud provisions, impose combined disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties exceeding $1.1 million, and bar them from most securities activities and association with brokers or dealers, except for trading in their personal accounts. The SEC‚??s investigation and litigation were handled by staff from the Miami Regiona

documents.title: Nathan Gauvin; Blackridge, LLC; Gray Digital Capital Management USA, LLC; Gray Digital Technologies, LLC
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
keywords: Gray Digital Capital Management USA LLC
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed a civil enforcement action in the Eastern District of New York against Canadian citizen Nathan Gauvin and three entities he controls‚??Blackridge, LLC, Gray Digital Capital Management USA, LLC, and Gray Digital Technologies, LLC‚??alleging two fraudulent securities offerings that raised over $18 million from U.S. and foreign retail investors. The complaint claims Gauvin built a following on Discord by falsely holding himself out as a successful investment professional managing over $1 billion through Blackridge, a shell company, and then conducted an unregistered offering of interests in the so‚??called Gray Fund. He and Gray Digital allegedly misrepresented the fund‚??s performance and assets, claiming double‚??digit monthly returns and over $78 million in assets, when actual returns were about 1.4% monthly and assets were substantially lower, and diverted approximately $6.3 million for luxury personal spending. In a second scheme, beginning May 2024, Gauvin allegedly offered "seed stock" in Gray Digital Technologies at $30,000 per share based on fabricated valuations and revenue for a company that had no operations, assets, or revenue, raising at least $60,000 from two retail

documents.title: Marshall E. Melton and Integrated Consulting & Management, LLC
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained a final judgment against Greensboro resident Marshall E. Melton and his company, Integrated Consulting & Management, LLC, for operating a fraudulent securities offering. According to the SEC's complaint, filed in May 2023, Melton raised approximately $1.03‚??$1.49 million from seven investors‚??mostly elderly‚??based on false promises that funds would be used to buy and renovate properties in downtown Laurinburg, North Carolina, to generate rental income and resale proceeds. The court granted summary judgment for the SEC in April 2025, finding violations of Section 17(a) of the Securities Act, and Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 of the Exchange Act. The final judgment permanently enjoins the defendants from future violations, bars Melton from participating in most securities transactions (with narrow exceptions for listed or OTC-traded securities in his personal accounts), and imposes financial remedies, including joint and several disgorgement of $916,341 plus $312,460.84 in prejudgment interest and a $472,902 civil penalty against Melton.

documents.title: Rapid Therapeutic Science Laboratories, Inc. and Donal R. Schmidt, Jr.
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained final judgments against Rapid Therapeutic Science Laboratories, Inc. (RTSL) and its CEO, Donal R. Schmidt, Jr., for making false and misleading public statements about the company's business and stock. The misstatements concerned purported industry certifications, major sales contracts, lab standards compliance, the qualifications of RTSL's chief science officer, the safety and legality of its CBD inhalers, and the approval status of RTSL's Nasdaq listing application. Without admitting or denying the allegations, RTSL and Schmidt consented to permanent injunctions against future violations of antifraud, registration, reporting, and certification provisions of the federal securities laws. RTSL was ordered to pay $686,090 in disgorgement plus $183,528 in prejudgment interest. Schmidt was ordered to pay $144,285 in disgorgement, $38,596 in prejudgment interest, and a $236,451 civil penalty, and is subject to a five-year conduct-based injunction, as well as five-year officer/director and penny stock bars. The case was brought in the Northern District of Texas and litigated by staff in the SEC‚??s Fort Worth Regional Office.

documents.title: Oppenheimer & Co., Inc.
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC announced that the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York entered a final consent judgment against Oppenheimer & Co. Inc. concerning alleged failures to comply with municipal bond offering disclosure requirements. The SEC's complaint alleged that, between June 2017 and April 2022, Oppenheimer sold securities in hundreds of municipal offerings in purported reliance on the municipal "limited offering exemption" without meeting its conditions, made deceptive compliance representations to issuers, and lacked adequate policies and procedures to ensure adherence to the exemption when acting as underwriter. Without admitting or denying the allegations, Oppenheimer consented to a final judgment that permanently enjoins it from violating Exchange Act Rule 15c2-12, MSRB Rules G-17 and G-27, and Exchange Act Section 15B(c)(1), and requires payment of a $1.2 million civil penalty. The matter was investigated and litigated by SEC staff, with assistance from the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board.

documents.title: Thomas San Miguel
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained a final judgment against Thomas San Miguel, founder and former CEO of SGR Energy, Inc., for conducting an unregistered and fraudulent securities offering that raised about $21.3 million from over 300 investors. The SEC alleged that San Miguel misled investors with false promises of a 12% annual dividend, increasing revenues and profits, and a $19 million account receivable, and misrepresented the intended use of investor funds for expanding SGR Energy‚??s fuel-blending operations, including a purported Colombian terminal acquisition. Without admitting or denying the allegations, San Miguel consented to a judgment permanently enjoining him from violating key antifraud and registration provisions of the federal securities laws, imposing a conduct-based injunction, an officer-and-director bar, and a $700,000 civil penalty.

documents.title: FINRA Adopts Amendments to the Arbitration Codes to Accelerate the Processing of Arbitration Proceedings for Parties Who Qualify Based on Their Age or Health Condition
documents.speaker: FINRA

Effective for arbitrations filed on or after March 30, 2026, eligible parties can request accelerated processing at the time of filing a claim or answer if they are at least 70 years old or certify that a medical diagnosis and prognosis create a reasonable belief that faster processing is necessary to avoid prejudice. The Director of Dispute Resolution Services (DRS) will determine eligibility based on objective criteria without assessing the reasonableness of the party‚??s belief. documents.title: Division of Trading and Markets: Frequently Asked Questions ‚?? Rule 15c3-3 and Daily Customer and PAB Reserve Computations
documents.speaker: Division of Trading and Markets
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC Division of Trading and Markets staff FAQ clarifies several implementation issues related to Rule 15c3-3 daily customer and PAB reserve computations for carrying broker-dealers. Broker-dealers with average total credits of at least $500 million, calculated from the 12 month-end FOCUS reports from January 31, 2025 through December 31, 2025, must begin performing daily customer and PAB reserve computations by June 30, 2026. Firms may conduct non-binding "test" daily reserve computations to validate systems and procedures before commencing required or voluntary daily computations, provided these tests do not trigger reserve account withdrawals and are clearly documented as tests. For firms using the alternative net capital method under Rule 15c3-1(a)(1)(ii), those that voluntarily adopt daily customer reserve computations may apply the 2% aggregate debit items charge instead of 3% on or after March 14, 2025, if they give their DEA 30 days‚?? prior written notice. Firms required to perform daily customer reserve computations under Rule 15c3-3(e)(3)(i)(B)(1) may also use the 2% debit charge without any DEA pre-notification. documents.title: Global Research Analyst Settlement
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC Division of Enforcement has consented to terminate the remaining undertakings in the Addendum to the 2003 and 2004 Global Research Analyst Settlement final judgments against several major investment banks, subject to court approval. These undertakings were originally designed to address conflicts of interest between equity research analysts and investment banking personnel. The Addendum included a sunset provision anticipating that subsequently adopted rules would supersede these obligations, and it was previously revised by court order in 2010. Following the adoption and SEC approval of FINRA Rule 2241 in 2015, which governs research analysts and research reports and addresses such conflicts within broker-dealers, the settling firms moved in 2025 to terminate the remaining undertakings. In its court responses, the SEC cites the Addendum‚??s sunset provision and the existence of FINRA Rule 2241, states that it believes modification of the judgments is in the public interest, and consents to the requested modifications.

documents.title: Shahin Ahmed
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed a civil enforcement action against Shahin Ahmed, a personal driver for a hedge fund manager, alleging that he falsely posed as a professional money manager and defrauded three investors, causing losses exceeding $1 million between March 2020 and February 2022. According to the complaint, Ahmed misrepresented his experience, suggested that client funds would be invested by the hedge fund manager he worked for, fabricated an investment opportunity and account performance, and obtained access to clients' brokerage accounts where he traded securities, guaranteed "risk-free" investments, and collected fraudulent fees without covering losses. Ahmed agreed to a bifurcated settlement, subject to court approval, providing for permanent injunctions against future violations of specified provisions of the Securities Act, Exchange Act, and Investment Advisers Act, a bar from most securities activities and from acting as or associating with an investment adviser, with disgorgement, interest, and penalties to be determined later. Separately, the Nassau County District Attorney's Office arraigned Ahmed on a state grand larceny charge related to one client. The SEC investigation and

documents.title: Gregoire P. Tournant; Trevor L. Taylor; Stephen G. Bond-Nelson
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained final civil judgments against former Allianz Global Investors U.S. LLC portfolio managers Gregoire P. Tournant, Trevor L. Taylor, and Stephen G. Bond-Nelson for a multi‚??year fraudulent scheme involving the Structured Alpha options strategy. The SEC alleged they misled investors about downside risks and performance, affecting roughly $11 billion in investments and over $550 million in fees, by manipulating financial reports and other information. In parallel criminal cases, all three received probation, home confinement for two of them, fines, and substantial forfeiture amounts. In the SEC action, and without admitting or denying the allegations, Tournant consented to injunctive relief, a permanent industry bar, and disgorgement of $17.6 million; Taylor and Bond‚??Nelson had previously agreed to injunctions and industry bars. Ordered disgorgement for all three was deemed satisfied by the criminal forfeiture orders. The matter was handled by the SEC‚??s Complex Financial Instruments Unit, with assistance from the U.S. Attorney‚??s Office for the Southern District of New York and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service.

documents.title: James R. Collins and Robert F. DiMeo
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
keywords: Section 17(a) of the Securities Act of 1933
Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934
United States v. Collins et al., 20-cr-232
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained a final judgment against former Honor Finance, LLC executives James R. Collins and Robert F. DiMeo for fraud related to a $100 million subprime automobile loan securitization (Honor Automobile Trust Securitization 2016-1). The SEC alleged they artificially inflated collateral values by including ineligible loans, extending repayment dates without borrower knowledge, and forgiving payments owed by delinquent borrowers, resulting in false servicing and performance information to investors. The court permanently enjoined them from violating antifraud provisions of the Securities Act and Exchange Act, imposed permanent officer-and-director bars, and ordered disgorgement and prejudgment interest totaling $550,332 for Collins and $198,731 for DiMeo, deemed satisfied by a prior criminal restitution order. In the related criminal case, they were jointly ordered to pay $67,243,790.94 in restitution; Collins received a 48‚??month prison sentence, and DiMeo received one day of imprisonment and 12 months of supervised release.

documents.title: FINRA Adopts Amendments to Rule 6730 (Transaction Reporting) to Streamline Allocation Reporting for BD/IAs
documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA has amended TRACE transaction reporting Rule 6730 to allow firms that operate as both broker-dealers and investment advisers (BD/IAs) to report certain allocation trades to managed customer accounts on an aggregated basis rather than submitting separate TRACE reports for each individual account allocation. New Supplementary Material .08 permits a BD/IA, at its option, to file a single aggregate TRACE report covering multiple allocations of an aggregate order in a TRACE-eligible security to managed customer accounts, provided the allocations share the same price and time of execution, and the report is submitted within existing TRACE timeframes. The aggregate report must include the number of managed customer accounts receiving allocations, and FINRA will disseminate both the number of accounts and the aggregate allocated volume (subject to existing size caps). documents.title: Yida Gao and Shima Capital Management LLC
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed fraud charges against Shima Capital Management LLC and its owner, Yida Gao, alleging they made false and misleading statements to raise over $169.9 million from investors for a crypto-asset venture fund and a BitClout-focused special purpose vehicle. In the BitClout SPV offering, Gao allegedly told investors he would buy BitClout tokens at a 20‚??40% discount to protect their investments but instead sold the tokens to the SPV at a higher price, retaining $1.9 million in undisclosed profit. The SEC charged violations of antifraud provisions under the Securities Act, Exchange Act, and Advisers Act. Gao consented to a bifurcated settlement including a permanent injunction, disgorgement of approximately $3.92 million plus interest (offset by any criminal restitution), and future determination of penalties and bars, while Shima Capital agreed to a permanent injunction and compliance undertakings; both settlement

documents.title: Srinivas Koneru
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC has filed a civil enforcement action against Srinivas Koneru, founder and former owner of Triterras Fintech Pte. Ltd., alleging he engaged in a fraudulent scheme related to the November 2020 SPAC merger between Triterras Fintech and Netfin Acquisition Corp. The complaint alleges Koneru misrepresented the performance and third‚??party financing activity on Triterras‚??s Kratos platform, particularly its Trade Finance module, by overstating the involvement and financing volume of ten lending funds and by including loans after the fact to create a false impression they originated on the platform. The SEC charges Koneru with violations of the antifraud provisions of the Securities Act and Exchange Act and seeks permanent injunctive relief, disgorgement with prejudgment interest, civil penalties, and an officer‚??and‚??director bar.

documents.title: Andrew Scott Corbman
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained a final judgment against former registered representative and investment adviser Andrew Scott Corbman for operating a $4.15 million fraudulent scheme from 2019 to 2023. Corbman allegedly induced investors, including retired military officers and a retired federal civil servant, to invest over $4 million in securities structured as "Loan Agreements" using false and misleading statements about his track record, the risk profile of the investments, and the intended use of funds. The complaint states that his trading actually incurred losses exceeding $3 million and that he failed to disclose his prior personal bankruptcy, extensive FINRA disciplinary history leading to disbarment and fines, and loss of his Virginia insurance license after a state regulatory investigation. Instead of investing as promised, he allegedly engaged in extremely high‚??risk trading and misappropriated investor money to pay personal expenses including back taxes, credit card debt, and attorney fees related to his bankruptcy. documents.title: Virtu Financial, Inc.; Virtu Americas LLC
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC Division of Enforcement announced that the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York entered a final consent judgment against broker-dealer Virtu Americas LLC in a civil enforcement action alleging failures to maintain adequate policies and procedures to prevent misuse of customers' material nonpublic information (MNPI). The SEC's complaint claimed that between January 2018 and April 2019, Virtu Americas operated both a proprietary trading business and an institutional trade execution business but did not establish, maintain, and enforce safeguards reasonably designed to ensure that proprietary traders could not access MNPI from customer order databases. Without admitting or denying the allegations, Virtu Americas consented to a judgment permanently enjoining it from violating Section 15(g) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and requiring payment of a $2.5 million civil monetary penalty. In exchange, the SEC agreed to dismiss with prejudice all other claims and relief against Virtu Americas and all claims and relief against its parent company, Virtu Financial, Inc. The release also identifies the SEC staff responsible for the litigation and investigation

documents.title: Supervision and Regulation
documents.speaker: Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman
keywords: Economic Growth and Regulatory Paperwork Reduction Act
documents.enrichment_summary:
Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman testifies that the U.S. banking system remains sound and resilient, with strong capital, liquidity, lending growth, and profitability, while noting rising competitive pressure from nonbank financial institutions that are not subject to equivalent prudential standards. She outlines two main themes: current banking conditions and progress on her supervisory and regulatory priorities since confirmation.

Bowman emphasizes the need to empower regulated banks to compete with fintechs and digital asset firms by encouraging responsible innovation and clarifying regulatory treatment of digital assets and stablecoins, including forthcoming capital, liquidity, and diversification rules for stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act. She underscores that supervision must support innovation while maintaining safety and soundness.

A major priority is tailoring regulation for community banks. Bowman warns against pushing standards designed for the largest banks onto smaller, less complex institutions. She supports congressional efforts to raise outdated statutory and asset thresholds and to modernize Bank Secrecy Act and anti-money-laundering requireme

documents.title: Opening Remarks
documents.speaker: Chair Jerome H. Powell
documents.enrichment_summary: Chair Jerome H. Powell delivers commemorative remarks on the legacy of George P. Shultz, explicitly avoiding discussion of current economic conditions or monetary policy. Powell highlights Shultz as a role model who successfully combined private-sector work with extensive public service, holding four cabinet positions and engaging major policy issues of his era. He emphasizes Shultz's blend of firm principles, integrity, and practical problem-solving, including a strong belief in market mechanisms tempered by recognition of market failures that warrant public policy intervention. Powell notes Shultz's contributions across domains such as collective bargaining, wage and price controls, exchange rates, health care reform, climate change, and nuclear disarmament. He underscores Shultz's efforts to combat racial discrimination and expand opportunities for minorities, grounded in both moral and economic reasoning. documents.title: Solomon Lichtenstein

documents.title: AI, the Economy, and Financial Stability
documents.speaker: Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson
documents.enrichment_summary: Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson discusses how artificial intelligence (AI) may affect the Federal Reserve's dual mandate and financial stability. documents.title: Welcoming Remarks
documents.speaker: Governor Michael S. Barr
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Michael S. Barr delivers welcoming remarks at the 2025 National College Fed Challenge Finals, emphasizing the Federal Reserve's dual mandate of maximum employment and stable prices and the educational value of the competition. He congratulates the six finalist teams, notes the record participation and return to in‚??person finals in the FOMC meeting room, and draws parallels between the students' policy recommendations and the actual work of the FOMC, including challenges such as data delays from the government shutdown and the need for policy independence from short‚??term political pressures. documents.speaker: Governor Lisa D. Cook
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Lisa D. Cook argues that the U.S. financial system is currently resilient, but highlights several emerging vulnerabilities that warrant close monitoring. She links financial stability to the Federal Reserve's dual mandate, using the Great Recession and Michigan's experience as an example of how financial fragility can translate into severe job losses and household hardship. She identifies three near- to medium-term vulnerability areas: (1) elevated asset valuations across several markets, which increase the likelihood of outsized price declines but, in her view, do not currently threaten system-wide stability given strong balance sheets and bank capital; (2) rapid growth and rising complexity in private credit, which has expanded financing for privately held firms and may enhance stability when matched with long-term funding, but whose opacity, leverage, and interconnections with banks and insurers could transmit losses under stress; and (3) the growing footprint of leveraged hedge fund relative-value strategies in the U.S. Treasury market, which usually support liquidity but could magnify market dysfunction if funding conditions tighten and trades unwind abruptly. Santarelli, alleging he ran a multi‚??million‚??dollar, nationwide investment fraud through Norada Capital Management, LLC between June 2020 and June 2024. documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC filed a civil enforcement action in the Southern District of New York against Joshua Wander, Steven Pasko, Damien Alfalla, and entities 777 Partners LLC and 600 Partners LLC, alleging a multi‚??year fraud in connection with a $237 million preferred equity offering. documents.title: Cyrus P. Naderi

Jefferson outlines his outlook that U.S. economic growth remains moderate but has been temporarily dampened by a recent federal government shutdown, which has also delayed key data releases. documents.speaker: Governor Michael S. Barr
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Michael S. Barr outlines how artificial intelligence, particularly generative AI (GenAI), is reshaping the economy, the financial sector, and central banking. Jefferson discusses how rapidly advancing artificial intelligence (AI) is affecting, and may further affect, the Federal Reserve‚??s dual mandate of maximum employment and price stability, and briefly updates his U.S. economic and monetary policy outlook. Governor Lisa D. Cook assesses the U.S. economic outlook under the Fed's dual mandate amid a federal government shutdown that has disrupted key official data. documents.enrichment_summary: Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman delivers welcome remarks (via pre-recorded video) to the 2025 Federal Reserve Stress Testing Research Conference in Boston. She emphasizes the conference's role in advancing research on stress testing and highlights an upcoming, comprehensive Federal Reserve proposal to reform and enhance large-bank stress testing. The proposal will focus on greater transparency, detailed model descriptions and assumptions, public comment on model changes for the 2026 stress test, refinements to scenario design (including the severely adverse macroeconomic scenario and global market shock framework), and disclosure of macroeconomic modeling approaches. These reforms are framed as part of a broader effort to recalibrate capital requirements to balance safety and soundness with economic growth, reduce volatility in stress test results, and incorporate stakeholder input. Bowman concludes by acknowledging the work of Federal Reserve stress testing staff and the importance of ongoing collaboration among academics, regulators, and industry participants in building a more resilient financial system.

He emphasizes that the key policy uncertainty is how the conflict between robust spending/GDP and weak job creation will be resolved in coming months. He highlights complications from a federal government shutdown that has delayed key data releases, the temporary nature of tariff-driven inflation, and a 'no hire, no fire' labor market dynamic in which firms are holding onto workers but not expanding hiring. documents.speaker: Governor Christopher J. Waller
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Christopher J. Waller argues that artificial intelligence is part of a long historical pattern of disruptive but ultimately beneficial technological change. He frames AI as accelerating three recurring dynamics: continuous disruption of work and social life, shifts in power away from incumbents toward broader groups, and long-run gains in productivity and living standards. Powell explains the structure, role, and recent evolution of the Federal Reserve's balance sheet, defends the ample-reserves implementation framework, and links these technical issues to current economic conditions and monetary policy decisions.
