documents.title: Agridime, LLC, Jed Wood, and Joshua Link
documents.speaker: SEC Division of Enforcement
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC obtained final judgments against Agridime, LLC and its founders, Jed Wood and Joshua Link, for operating a $191 million cattle-related Ponzi scheme from 2021 to 2023. The defendants sold investment contracts promising fixed-price cattle purchases and guaranteed returns of up to 32%, but failed to buy sufficient cattle and instead used investor funds to pay earlier investors and undisclosed commissions, including over $1.3 million each to Wood and to Link and his wife. The court had previously granted a temporary restraining order, asset freeze, and appointed a receiver. The final judgments permanently enjoin the defendants from violating antifraud and registration provisions of the federal securities laws, bar Wood and Link from serving as officers or directors or participating in securities offerings, and impose substantial disgorgement, prejudgment interest, and civil penalties, with Agridime‚??s disgorgement deemed satisfied by the receiver‚??s collections. The case was litigated by staff from the SEC‚??s Fort Worth Regional Office.

documents.enrichment_summary: Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson discusses recent revisions to the Federal Reserve's monetary policy framework and their application to the current U.S. economic outlook. He stresses continuity with past practice, including the 2 percent inflation objective and forward-looking policy. documents.title: Economic Outlook
documents.speaker: Chair Jerome H. Powell
documents.enrichment_summary: Chair Jerome H. Powell describes a U.S. economy that is moderating but still resilient amid shifting trade, immigration, fiscal, regulatory, and geopolitical conditions. GDP growth has slowed to around 1.5 percent in the first half of the year due mainly to softer consumer spending, with weak housing but stronger business investment in equipment and intangibles. The labor market has become less dynamic, with slower job gains and a slight rise in unemployment to 4.3 percent, increasing downside risks to employment even as some labor indicators remain stable. Inflation has fallen sharply from its 2022 peak but has recently picked up to 2.7 percent (headline PCE) and 2.9 percent (core PCE), largely attributed to higher tariffs and viewed as a likely one-time price-level shift spread over several quarters rather than a persistent inflation surge. Near-term risks are seen as tilted toward higher inflation and weaker employment, creating a complex tradeoff for monetary policy. documents.title: FINRA Adopts Exemption From FINRA Rules 5130 and 5131 for Business Development Companies
documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA Regulatory Notice 25-08 announces amendments to FINRA Rules 5130 and 5131 to create a new general exemption for business development companies (BDCs). Non-traded and private BDCs, defined by Section 2(a)(48) of the Investment Company Act, are exempted from Rule 5130 and the spinning provisions in Rule 5131(b), provided they are not formed or maintained for the specific purpose of allowing restricted persons to invest in new issues. Traded BDCs remain covered by the existing general exemption for publicly traded entities. The amendments aim to align the treatment of non-traded and private BDCs with registered investment companies and traded BDCs, enabling BDCs to access IPO allocations more easily while maintaining protections around the integrity of the public offering process. The effective date of the amendments is July 23, 2025.

documents.title: Spare the Trees So Investors Can See the Forest: Remarks before the Executive Compensation Roundtable
documents.speaker: Hester M. Peirce
documents.enrichment_summary: Commissioner Hester M. Peirce argues that the SEC's current executive compensation disclosure regime has become excessively detailed, costly, and of limited value to investors, focusing on granular and sometimes immaterial items ("random trees") instead of providing a coherent, decision-useful overview (the "forest"). She questions whether rules such as pay ratio and pay-versus-performance disclosures, often mandated by Dodd-Frank and layered into Item 402 of Regulation S-K, genuinely furnish a rational basis for investment decisions or merely satisfy public curiosity. Peirce emphasizes that the growing complexity and volume of these disclosures consume significant corporate resources, distort executive pay design, and may even lead companies to alter or eliminate beneficial practices (like certain security measures or perks) solely to avoid adverse optics in disclosures. She calls for reassessing and potentially scaling back or refining executive compensation disclosure requirements so they better align with materiality, reflect economic reality, and protect investors without directing corporate behavior or imposing a "regulatory tax" devoid of corresponding investor benefit.

documents.speaker: Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman
documents.enrichment_summary:
Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman outlines a pragmatic, risk-focused agenda to reshape Federal Reserve supervision and regulation. She emphasizes tailoring supervision and regulatory standards to bank size, complexity, and business model, particularly by better distinguishing community and small banks from larger institutions and revisiting rigid asset thresholds like the $10 billion community bank cutoff. Bowman plans to enhance supervision by re-centering examiner attention on material financial risks (credit, interest rate, liquidity), recalibrating ratings frameworks to align more closely with banks‚?? financial condition, scrutinizing the use and transparency of horizontal reviews, and revisiting supervisory guidance to support clarity and innovation (including digital assets and AI). She stresses upgrading examiner training and expanding commissioning to more supervisory staff to sustain expertise amid an aging workforce.

documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Lisa D. Cook delivers brief welcoming remarks at a Fed Listens event hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta. documents.speaker: Governor Lisa D. Cook

documents.title: Commencement Remarks
documents.speaker: Governor Adriana D. Kugler
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Adriana D. Kugler delivers commencement remarks to UC Berkeley economics graduates, blending reflections from her younger and current self. She emphasizes that economics is a powerful but evolving tool rather than a belief system, and urges graduates to actively engage in the "marketplace of ideas" to advance broadly accepted, foundational economic principles that promote prosperity. Kugler highlights the importance of expertise amid disinformation, citing Jonathan Rauch's concept of an unwritten "constitution of knowledge" that helps societies distinguish truth from falsehood. Acknowledging the difficult environment for academic and public-service careers, she nonetheless encourages graduates to cultivate impatience, stubborn determination, and public-spirited purpose, drawing on her own path through academia, government, and international institutions. She closes by affirming the value of a Berkeley economics education and calling on graduates to use their training to make the world better.

He describes U.S. design choices around collateral, pricing, and penalties (e.g., fully collateralized discount window, penalty rates on overnight overdrafts) and compares them with similar facilities at the Bank of England, Bank of Japan, and European Central Bank. The cross‚??jurisdiction review highlights tradeoffs between interest rate levels and collateral eligibility, different frameworks (ample‚??reserves vs. repo‚??led), and how facilities scale up sharply during crises but remain modestly used in normal times. Pandemic-induced labor shortages pushed firms to adopt efficiency-enhancing innovations, such as online ordering and self‚??checkout, which raised potential GDP, eased price pressures, and reduced the need for demand‚??dampening monetary policy. Cook then examines two unfolding, opposing forces on future productivity: recent trade policy changes and the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI). documents.title: Thank You, John
documents.speaker: Governor Christopher J. Waller
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Christopher J. Waller reflects on how John Taylor‚??s work on rules versus discretion in monetary policy, and specifically Taylor‚??s 1983 commentary on Barro and Gordon, inspired Waller‚??s own 20‚??year research program on central bank institutional design. He traces the evolution from Kydland and Prescott‚??s time‚??inconsistency problem and Barro‚??Gordon‚??s reputation model, through Rogoff‚??s argument for a more inflation‚??averse ("conservative") central banker and Alesina‚??s partisan business cycles, to Waller‚??s own work on central bank boards with staggered, long, and independent terms. Waller argues that credibility is more robust when embedded in institutions rather than in individuals, and that an independent, board‚??based central bank structure‚??like the Federal Reserve‚??s Board of Governors‚??can balance democratic accountability (via appointments) with macroeconomic stability (via insulation from short‚??term political pressures). He credits John Taylor‚??s single line about society finding institutional solutions to time inconsistency for launching his research journey and closes by affirming the value and durability of the Fed‚??s current governance model.

documents.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market: A Scenario-Based Approach
documents.speaker: Governor Michael S. Barr
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Michael S. Barr analyzes how artificial intelligence, especially generative AI, could reshape the labor market and interact with U.S. monetary policy. He opens with the current U.S. macroeconomic outlook, warning that unprecedented tariffs are likely to raise inflation, slow growth, disrupt supply chains, and increase unemployment, complicating Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) decisions. He then characterizes AI, and in particular generative and emerging agentic AI, as a likely general purpose technology analogous to railroads or electricity, with broad productivity potential but uncertain labor-market effects. Barr sets out two scenarios. Jobs remain plentiful, productivity and real wages rise, and labor force participation may increase, though some workers experience dislocation, inequality may widen via skill-biased technological change, and capital owners may capture outsized gains. Drawing on her own unexpected path from philosophy student to Federal Reserve governor, she encourages graduates to remain optimistic amid uncertainty, to stay intellectually curious, to treat learning and preparation as lifelong pursuits (including engaging thoughtfully with emerging technologies like artificial intelligence), and to seek out diverse forms of service to the greater good. She situates these guides in the college's civic-minded culture and her own record of public service, concluding with a call for graduates to embrace risk, pursue big questions, and apply their skills and values in an unpredictable but opportunity-filled world.

documents.title: Inflation Dynamics and the Phillips Curve
documents.speaker: Governor Adriana D. Kugler
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Adriana D. Kugler delivered an economics lecture at Harvard University on April 7, 2025, explaining recent U.S. inflation dynamics and the role of the Phillips curve in modeling them. She describes pandemic-era inflation as occurring in waves‚??first food, then core goods, then core services, and finally housing‚??and links these patterns to sector-specific factors such as shortages, demand rotation to goods, wages, and housing rents. The lecture then uses the Phillips curve framework, including wage and expectations-augmented versions, to analyze how inflation relates to labor market slack, expectations, and other drivers. Kugler reviews empirical results across different periods (1960‚??1986 vs. 1987‚??2019), presents a baseline and updated Phillips curve models, and shows dynamic simulations, including models that incorporate the vacancy-to-unemployment ratio and measures of shortages, in an effort to better capture the most recent inflation episode.

documents.enrichment_summary:
Governor Michael S. Barr outlines how generative AI (Gen AI), banks, and fintechs intersect, emphasizing that Gen AI could become a competitive necessity in banking but must be integrated responsibly. He argues that banking is inherently data-driven and that Gen AI can improve document analysis, credit underwriting, customer service via advanced chatbots, and trading/analytics. Despite this potential, banks have moved cautiously due to model immaturity (hallucinations, stochastic outputs), strict requirements for precision and explainability, information-security and privacy risks, and internal tech debt and siloed data.

Barr contrasts fintechs‚?? speed, clean tech stacks, and single-product focus with banks‚?? scale, rich customer data, diversified business lines, and mature risk controls. He frames the bank‚??fintech dynamic as a race between speed (fintechs) and scale (banks), suggesting that both competition and collaboration (e.g., partnerships, investments, vendor relationships) will likely accelerate Gen AI adoption in financial services. This acceleration, he argues, can benefit consumers via better, cheaper, and faster financial services, provided that risks are well managed.

Barr emphasizes the central role of small businesses in the U.S. economy, highlighting their contributions to GDP, employment, and job creation, as well as rapid growth among women- and minority-owned firms. documents.speaker: Governor Christopher J. Waller
documents.enrichment_summary: Governor Christopher J. Waller explains that at the latest FOMC meeting he supported keeping the federal funds target range unchanged while favoring continuation of the current pace of reductions in the Federal Reserve's securities holdings. He argues that balance sheet reduction remains important for normalizing monetary policy and lowering excess reserves, noting that current reserve balances above $3 trillion indicate an abundant, not merely ample, level of reserves. He sees no signs from money market indicators or outreach that reserves are nearing an ample level, and therefore believes it is premature to slow or stop redemptions beyond the pace already reduced in June 2024. Waller emphasizes that if unexpected strains in reserve demand arise, the Fed should use existing tools and have a clear contingency plan to inject reserves swiftly, rather than altering the ongoing pace of balance sheet runoff. He frames this as a procedural and process issue, asserting that robust contingency planning supports market stability and the FOMC's macroeconomic objectives.

documents.title: FINRA Reminds Members of its Policy Prohibiting Members From Recording FINRA Calls and Meetings
documents.speaker: FINRA
keywords: just and equitable principles of trade
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA reaffirms and updates its longstanding policy that member firms and their associated persons are prohibited from making audio or video recordings of conversations, calls, or meetings with FINRA staff conducted in connection with examinations, investigations, or any other oversight functions, including through automated recording or AI/virtual meeting tools. FINRA cites concerns about potential editing or alteration of recordings, inaccuracies in AI-generated transcripts or summaries, and consistency with FINRA Rule 2010 and certain state consent-to-recording laws. Members should not expect FINRA to consent to recording, which will only be allowed in rare circumstances. FINRA also states that, as a general matter, its own staff will not record such interactions without consent from the parties.

The notice emphasizes both opportunities (e.g., enhanced analysis, investor education, surveillance, and operational efficiency) and risks (e.g., accuracy, privacy, bias, intellectual property, and misuse by threat actors). It highlights supervisory obligations under Rule 3110, stressing that firms using Gen AI in supervision, communications, or other functions must maintain reasonably designed supervisory systems and policies that address technology governance, model risk management, data privacy and integrity, and model reliability and accuracy. documents.title: FINRA Adopts Amendments Relating to Protected Option and Warrant Positions Under FINRA Rule 4210
documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA has amended Rule 4210 (Margin Requirements) to add a specific exception for certain "protected" short index option or warrant positions that are hedged with products tracking the same underlying index. When a short index call or put option (or warrant) is carried in an account and is offset by a qualifying long or short position in an underlying stock basket, non-leveraged index mutual fund, or non-leveraged ETF based on the same index, the short option or warrant position is excluded from the standard margin requirements in Rule 4210(f)(2)(E)(i) and (f)(2)(E)(iii), provided certain coverage and maintenance conditions are met. The protection must initially equal at least 100% of the aggregate current underlying index value at trade creation (measured either at order entry/execution or close of business that day), must not fall below 95% of the aggregate current underlying index value thereafter, and margin must be maintained as the greater of: (1) any amount by which the aggregate index value exceeds (for calls) or is below (for puts) the aggregate exercise price, or (2) any amount by which the protection falls below 100% of the aggregate index value. documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA, in consultation with the U.S. Department of the Treasury, has adopted amendments to enhance post-trade transparency for U.S. Treasury securities by creating two new TRACE data products focused on on-the-run nominal coupon Treasuries. Beginning March 25, 2024, FINRA will disseminate an end-of-day transaction file with capped trade sizes, providing price, size (subject to caps), counterparty type, ATS flags, and other modifiers for trades reported that day, while omitting any party-identifying information. Beginning April 1, 2024, FINRA will also offer a Historic TRACE Data Set for Treasuries on a six-month delay with uncapped sizes, initially covering Q1 2019 through Q3 2023 and then updated quarterly. Non-professionals can access next-day, transaction-level data for free on FINRA‚??s website for personal, non-commercial use, while professionals can subscribe to the end-of-day and historic data sets for specified monthly and annual fees consistent with existing TRACE pricing for other asset classes. No new reporting obligations are imposed on TRACE reporters.

documents.title: FINRA Reminds Member Firms of Net Capital, Recordkeeping and Financial Reporting Requirements in Connection with Revenue Recognition Practices
documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA alerts member firms that misapplication of ASC 606 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers) in recognizing fees from customer contracts has led to violations of SEA Rules 15c3-1 (Net Capital), 17a-3 (Recordkeeping), and 17a-5 (Financial Reporting). Examinations found firms prematurely recognizing non-refundable M&A fees as revenue without performing or documenting the ASC 606-required performance obligation analysis, causing overstated revenues, understated liabilities and non-allowable assets, and in some cases net capital deficiencies or material reductions in excess net capital. FINRA instructs firms to adopt and consistently apply documented ASC 606-compliant revenue recognition policies; analyze each contract to identify performance obligations and when they are satisfied; maintain required books and records; and ensure FOCUS reports, Supplemental Statement of Income filings, and annual reports (including ASC 606 footnote disclosures) are all prepared in conformity with ASC 606 and SEA Rule 17a-5.

documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA announces that, effective November 30, 2023, it will discontinue collecting data from clearing and self-clearing firms under Rule 4540, which historically supported the Integrated National Surveillance and Information Technology Enhancements (INSITE) program. The decision is driven by the availability of alternative data sources‚??such as CAT data, supplemental FOCUS reports under Rule 4524, and margin statistics under Rule 4521(d)‚??that either replicate or improve upon the information previously gathered, enabling more granular risk assessment. documents.title: FINRA Adopts TAF Exemption for Proprietary Trading Firms
documents.speaker: FINRA
keywords: Options Order Protection and Locked/Crossed Market Plan
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA has amended its By-Laws to exempt proprietary trading firms from paying the Trading Activity Fee (TAF) on transactions executed on national securities exchanges where they hold membership. This change, effective November 6, 2023, is designed to align with recent SEC amendments to Exchange Act Rule 15b9-1, which will require many proprietary trading firms to become FINRA members if they conduct trading off of their member exchanges. Under the new TAF exemption, a proprietary trading firm must (i) trade only its own capital, (ii) have no customers other than brokers or dealers (including a six‚??month lookback), and (iii) conduct all trading through firm or affiliate accounts by owners, employees, or contractors. Trades executed off a member exchange, or on exchanges where the firm is not a member, remain subject to TAF unless another exemption applies. Both newly joining and existing FINRA member proprietary trading firms that meet these conditions are eligible for the exemption.

documents.title: Regulation T and SEA Rule 15c3-3 Extension of Time Requests Under a T+1 Settlement Cycle
documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA informs member firms that, in connection with the SEC's amendment of Exchange Act Rule 15c6-1(a) to move from a T+2 to a T+1 standard settlement cycle effective May 28, 2024, it is updating its Regulatory Extension (REX) system for Regulation T and SEA Rule 15c3-3(n) extension of time requests. For trades with dates prior to May 28, 2024, firms must continue using a T+4 payment period when requesting Regulation T extensions; beginning May 31, 2024, Regulation T extensions must be filed based on a T+1 settlement cycle, which shortens the payment period from T+4 to T+3. The notice describes updates to the REX Customer Test Environment (CTE), including specific implementation dates aligned with DTCC T+1 test cycles, batch and online form testing processes, SFTP file locations, and availability of reports through FINRA Gateway. FINRA also provides an updated 2024 Margin Extension Schedule, points firms to its Margin Regulation resources, and provides contacts for technical and regulatory questions.

documents.title: Amendments to Covered Agency Transaction Requirements under FINRA Rule 4210; Announcement of Effective Date
documents.speaker: FINRA
keywords: excess net mark to market loss
capital charge in lieu of margin
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA Regulatory Notice 23-14 announces SEC-approved amendments to the Covered Agency Transaction requirements under FINRA Rule 4210, effective May 22, 2024. The amendments modify margin rules for transactions such as TBAs, Specified Pool Transactions, and certain CMOs with forward settlement dates. Key changes include: (1) eliminating the 2% maintenance margin requirement for non-exempt accounts and applying a unified regime where members must collect margin only for each counterparty's excess net mark to market loss (above $250,000), regardless of exempt or non-exempt status; (2) allowing members, under strict conditions and quantitative caps, to take net capital charges instead of collecting margin on unmargined excess net mark to market losses, particularly for non-margin counterparties; and (3) streamlining and clarifying rule text, preserving the $250,000 de minimis transfer and $10 million gross open position exceptions (reframed via the new "small cash counterparty" definition), and consolidating risk limit and concentration threshold provisions. documents.title: FINRA Amends Its Rules to Allow Video Conference Hearings Before the Office of Hearing Officers and the National Adjudicatory Council Under Specified Conditions
documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA permanently amends several procedural rules to allow the Office of Hearing Officers (OHO) and the National Adjudicatory Council (NAC) to conduct evidentiary and oral argument hearings by video conference under specified conditions, expanding prior temporary COVID-19 measures. In-person hearings remain the default, but OHO and NAC may now order video hearings sua sponte when in‚??person proceedings would endanger health or safety or be impracticable (e.g., natural disasters, terrorism), and may also act on party motions. For NAC oral arguments, video conferences may also be ordered for other reasons, subject to parties showing any material disadvantage from remote format. The amendments apply to disciplinary, membership, eligibility, funding portal eligibility, TCDO/PCDO proceedings, and NAC appeals, and become effective August 23, 2023.

documents.title: FINRA Requests Comment on a Proposal to Require Members to Provide Rule 605 Order Execution Quality Reports to FINRA for Centralized Publication
documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA proposes to require all member firms that operate market centers subject to Rule 605 of Regulation NMS to provide their monthly order execution quality reports directly to FINRA so that FINRA can publish them in a single, centralized, freely accessible location on its website. The proposal is intended to supplement, not replace, existing Rule 605 obligations and to reduce search and access costs for investors, regulators, academics, and other users. FINRA presents an economic impact assessment, identifying expected benefits from improved accessibility and comparability of execution quality data, as well as anticipated implementation and ongoing compliance costs for members (e.g., programming, systems, vendor coordination). FINRA requests detailed public comment, including empirical support where possible, on the usefulness of centralization, potential gaps (such as non-FINRA member market centers and exchanges), possible investor tools and educational efforts, implementation challenges, and timing for systems changes.

documents.title: FINRA Adopts Amendments to FINRA Rule 8312 to Release Information on BrokerCheck Relating to Designation as a Restricted Firm
documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA has amended Rule 8312 (FINRA BrokerCheck Disclosure), effective June 1, 2023, to require public disclosure on BrokerCheck of whether a current or former member firm is designated as a "Restricted Firm" under Rules 4111 (Restricted Firm Obligations) and 9561 (Procedures for Regulating Activities Under Rule 4111). Rule 4111 establishes an annual, multi-step process to identify firms with a significant history of misconduct that pose a high degree of risk to investors and to impose a Restricted Deposit Requirement and/or operational conditions or restrictions on such firms. Rule 9561 provides expedited procedures to implement Rule 4111, and a firm‚??s Restricted Firm designation remains effective and visible on BrokerCheck during any related expedited proceeding, with an indication when the designation is on appeal. The change aims to enhance investor protection by alerting investors to the Restricted Firm status on both summary and detailed BrokerCheck reports and to further incentivize high-risk firms to change behaviors to avoid or remove such designation.

documents.title: FINRA Revises the Research Analyst (Series 86/87) Exam Program
documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA has revised the Research Analyst qualification exam program (Series 86/87), effective May 15, 2023, to better align with current research analyst job functions and relevant regulations. The revisions reorganize the exam into five explicit job functions across two parts (Series 86 and 87), update the content outline and legal/regulatory coverage, reduce the number of scored questions on Series 86 from 100 to 85 while maintaining exam length, and adjust question distribution by function. FINRA added FINRA Rule 5280 and removed Rule 2220 from the tested rule set, and confirmed via psychometric analysis that the shortened Series 86 exam reliably assesses required entry-level proficiency. The revised content outline is available on FINRA‚??s website and applies to exams administered on or after May 15, 2023.

documents.title: Frequently Asked Questions Regarding Rule Amendments to Broker-Dealer, Security-Based Swap Dealer, and Major Security-Based Swap Participant Electronic Recordkeeping Requirements
documents.speaker: Division of Trading and Markets
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC Division of Trading and Markets FAQ explains implementation details for recent amendments to Exchange Act Rule 17a-4 governing electronic recordkeeping for broker-dealers, including those registered as SBSDs and MSBSPs. The staff clarifies that, as of the January 3, 2023 effective date, firms may (1) begin using the new audit-trail alternative to the existing WORM (write once, read many) requirement for electronic records, and (2) replace the previously required "designated third party" with a "designated executive officer" for undertaking obligations related to access to and provision of electronic records. The FAQ stresses that these are staff views, not binding Commission rules, and that full compliance with the amended rule, including paragraph (i), is required by the May 3, 2023 compliance date.

documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA is re-opening the comment period for Regulatory Notice 15-13 in light of the SEC‚??s 2022 re-proposal to amend Exchange Act Rule 15b9-1, which would significantly narrow the exemption from membership in a national securities association for proprietary trading firms. If the SEC adopts the amendments, proprietary trading firms currently relying on Rule 15b9-1 would generally be required to register with FINRA, making FINRA‚??s existing fee structure, including the Trading Activity Fee (TAF), applicable to them. Regulatory Notice 15-13 had proposed an exemption from the TAF for transactions by proprietary trading firms on exchanges of which they are members, and FINRA now seeks renewed public comment on whether this exemption (or alternatives such as a different TAF rate for proprietary firms) is appropriate, equitable across members, and what economic, competitive, and behavioral impacts it may have on trading patterns, liquidity, and market functioning.

documents.title: FINRA Adopts Amendments to Require Reporting of Transactions in U.S. Dollar-Denominated Foreign Sovereign Debt Securities to TRACE
documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA Regulatory Notice 22-28 announces amendments to the TRACE Rule 6700 Series that will require member firms to report transactions in U.S. dollar-denominated foreign sovereign debt securities to TRACE, effective November 6, 2023. Foreign sovereign debt securities are defined as debt issued or guaranteed by a foreign government, its political subdivisions (including state, provincial, or municipal governments), or supranational entities. These trades must be reported on a same-day or next-business-day (T+1, as/of) basis depending on execution time, but will not be publicly disseminated. FINRA will update the TRACE security master list, provide a new report card for these securities, and instructs members to ensure systems and processes can identify TRACE-eligible transactions, even if not listed on the master list. FAQs clarify that only securities issued in U.S. dollars qualify, that reporting is required even where only ISIN/FIGI is available (via a TRACE New Issue Form), and that foreign municipal debt issued in U.S. dollars is included.

documents.title: FINRA Requests Comment on Proposed Changes to TRACE Reporting Relating to Delayed Treasury Spot Trades
documents.speaker: FINRA
documents.enrichment_summary: FINRA seeks public comment on proposed amendments to TRACE Rule 6730 to create a two-part reporting regime for delayed Treasury spot trades in corporate debt. Currently, such trades are only reported to TRACE once the dollar price is known, even though the key economic terms (spread to a benchmark U.S. Treasury and other terms) may have been agreed hours earlier. The proposal would require members to: (1) report, within 15 minutes of agreement, the spread to the benchmark U.S. Treasury, the identity of that benchmark (e.g., CUSIP), and other standard TRACE fields except dollar price; and (2) submit a supplemental report, within 15 minutes of the spotting time, with the calculated dollar price linked to the earlier report. Both reports would be immediately disseminated, providing the market with earlier and more complete information about the size and spread-based economics of delayed Treasury spot trades and clearly flagging that the final dollar price may not represent the then-current market price. documents.title: Frequently Asked Questions Regarding Security-Based Swaps
documents.speaker: Division of Trading and Markets
documents.enrichment_summary:
The SEC Division of Trading and Markets FAQ clarifies how the definition of "security-based swap" under Exchange Act Section 3(a)(68) applies to certain instruments. First, a futures or forward contract that allows for cash or physical settlement will not be treated as "intended to be physically settled"‚??and therefore will not be excluded from the definitions of "swap" and "security-based swap"‚??if, at the time of contract entry, the underlying securities cannot legally be transferred or are contractually restricted from transfer. For a deferred shipment or delivery contract to be considered intended to be physically settled, the underlying securities must, at contract inception, either be registered under Securities Act Section 5 or qualify for an applicable exemption, and any contractual transfer restrictions must be satisfied or waived.

Second, the staff states that a swap based on the shares of an exchange traded fund (ETF) or similar exchange-traded product that tracks a broad-based securities index (such as the S&P 500) is a security-based swap. documents.title: Frequently Asked Questions Regarding Submission of Applications and Notices In Lieu of Applications Pursuant to Commission Rule of Practice 194 (‚??Rule 194‚?ù)
documents.speaker: Division of Trading and Markets
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC Division of Trading and Markets staff FAQ explains how registered security-based swap dealers and major security-based swap participants (SBS Entities) should submit applications and notices under Commission Rule of Practice 194 for statutorily disqualified associated persons to effect or be involved in effecting security-based swaps. Rule 194 applications and notices must be filed with the SEC's Office of the Secretary via the dedicated email inbox, using specified subject lines that identify the SBS Entity and the associated person. Applications, including supporting materials, are generally kept confidential, subject to FOIA, the Exchange Act, and applicable SEC rules, while Commission orders granting or denying applications and all notices filed in lieu of applications are made public on the SEC website. Filers may attach supporting materials to notices and can request confidential treatment for information they do not want posted publicly. The FAQ emphasizes that it reflects staff views only and does not create legal obligations, and directs questions about Rule 194, applications, and notices to TM Staff via phone or email.

documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC Division of Trading and Markets staff clarifies procedural expectations for chief compliance officer (CCO) annual reports required under Exchange Act Rule 15Fk-1(c) for registered security-based swap dealers and major security-based swap participants. Registrants may, but are not required to, submit CCO Annual Reports through EDGAR, preferably as text-searchable PDFs. Both bank and non-bank registrants should submit the CCO Annual Report within 90 days after the end of their fiscal year, with the rule for non-banks tied to the deadline for annual financial reports. The FAQ also explains how registrants may request confidential treatment of CCO Annual Reports under Commission Rule 83, including marking requirements, FOIA-specific legends, and the need to provide contact information and deliver a separate written confidentiality request to the Office of FOIA Services by email, fax, or mail. The statement is expressly non-binding staff guidance that does not create new legal obligations or modify existing law.

documents.title: Staff Guidance on Automated Quotations under Regulation NMS
documents.speaker: Division of Trading and Markets
documents.enrichment_summary: The SEC Division of Trading and Markets staff provides guidance on what constitutes a de minimis intentional access delay for purposes of determining whether a trading center maintains an "automated quotation" under Rule 600(b)(3) and Rule 611 of Regulation NMS. While the Commission's June 17, 2016 interpretation allows de minimis intentional delays without defining a specific threshold, the staff states that intentional access delays of less than one millisecond are de minimis in today's market environment. Such delays are seen as consistent with the requirement that quotations be "immediate," because they fall within typical geographic and technological latencies experienced when routing orders between trading centers. The staff emphasizes that this is non-binding guidance, does not guarantee Commission approval of any particular delay or rule filing, and does not mean that all delays at or above one millisecond are necessarily non‚??de minimis. All proposed intentional access delays must still be filed with the Commission as rule changes, and the staff will revisit this guidance as technology and market conditions evolve.

Section 4(a)(4) protects only the broker's part of the transaction and is unavailable where the broker-dealer knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the customer's sale is not exempt (e.g., the customer is an underwriter or the sale is part of a distribution).
